vignette:
The Weight of Watching

Margaret is a 58-year-old widowed woman who spent most of her adult life as a homemaker and later as a part-time bookkeeper for a small hardware store, a job she quietly left two years ago and has not returned to since. She lives alone in the house she shared with her husband, Gerald, for thirty-one years, and she describes the rooms as feeling simultaneously too large and impossible to leave.

Three years ago, Margaret watched her husband of three decades suffer a massive stroke at their kitchen table. It was an ordinary Saturday morning — coffee, the newspaper, Gerald complaining mildly about his back. Then he made a sound she cannot find words for, a sound that lives somewhere beneath language, and he fell. She called 911 and then knelt beside him on the linoleum floor for eleven minutes, holding his hand, watching his face do things she was not prepared to see a face do. He died four days later in the ICU without regaining consciousness. Margaret was with him for all four of those days, and she was holding his hand when his breathing stopped.

She describes the weeks immediately following Gerald's death as strangely manageable — there was so much to do, so many people in the house, decisions that required her attention. It was approximately six weeks after the funeral, once the casseroles stopped arriving and the phone grew quiet, that something shifted. She began waking at three in the morning, heart hammering, certain she had heard that sound again. She would find herself standing in the kitchen, unable to explain how she got there, staring at the chair where Gerald had been sitting.

She stopped using the kitchen table altogether. She eats standing at the counter or in front of the television, and she has pushed Gerald's chair against the far wall with its back facing outward, though she cannot bring herself to remove it entirely. The linoleum has been covered with a large area rug she purchased in a kind of fugue state, dragging it home in her car and laying it down alone at midnight.

Margaret no longer reads the newspaper. She tells herself it is because she lost the habit, but she knows it is because Gerald read the newspaper. She has stopped answering calls from her daughter in Vancouver with any regularity, finding conversation exhausting in ways she cannot explain. She used to enjoy grocery shopping — she was the kind of woman who knew everyone at the store — but now she goes only when absolutely necessary, moving quickly through the aisles and avoiding eye contact, her chest tight, her mind scanning constantly for something she cannot name.

She describes a persistent sense that something terrible is always about to happen. She checks the locks three or four times before bed. She has stopped driving on the highway after an incident in which she became convinced, suddenly and completely, that the car was about to veer off the road — not that she wanted it to, but that it simply would, the way Gerald simply fell. Control, she has come to understand, is something she no longer fully believes in.

Sleep, when it comes, is thin and unreliable. The dreams are not always about Gerald — sometimes they are about nothing recognizable, just a feeling of enormous pressure and the inability to move or speak. She wakes exhausted and lies in bed listening to the house settle, cataloguing sounds.

What Margaret finds most difficult to articulate, and what she returns to in quieter moments, is not the grief, which she understands and expects, but the way the memory of those eleven minutes on the kitchen floor seems to exist outside of time — always present tense, always happening, as though some part of her never stood up from that linoleum, and is kneeling there still, waiting to see what comes next.
